  the main types of ‘tile’


There are two basic forms of tile, both symmetri-
cally curved at right angles to their longitudinal
axis. The ﬁ rst, a plain or ‘plate’ tile, banwa 㜧䒎, is
squarer in shape with a slight curvature and longi-
tudinal taper (Fig. 3.04), and the second, a so-called
cylindrical tile, tongwa 䫺䒎, which is narrower,
parallel-sided and semi-circular in cross section
(Figs. 3.05 and 3.06).
   The banwa can be used alone, as it often is in the
north, when it is laid convex-side-down with an
overlap down the pitch of the roof and butted up to
and in register with the tiles on either side. In an ex-
ample of this laying pattern seen in Fig. 3.07 at Xi-
antongsi in Wutaishan, the butt seam between the
tiles is already quite weather-tight, although for
added protection a continuous bead of mortar may
be applied over the seam.
  On higher quality roofs, and more convention-
ally, tongwa are laid concave-face-downwards over
the seam between adjacent banwa, effectively re-
placing the mortar beading with a protective piece
that is more ‘ﬁnished’ in appearance. This is seen
here in a courtyard at the (vernacular) Wang family
mansion in Lingshi (Fig. 3.08).
   The changing curvature and occasionally steep
pitch of a traditional roof requires that precautions
be taken against tile-slippage and wind-chatter.
Banwa are naturally anchored by having a broad
surface area in contact with the lime mortar be-
neath, and also by being bonded to the adjacent
tiles above and below. However, tongwa rest large-
ly on their down-turned edges, and have a smaller
adhesive area for mortar. Some are therefore
pegged in place with nails, not randomly but along
prescribed rows according to rules ﬁ rst described
in the YZFS. These rules take account of the steep-
ness of pitch and span of the roof (see Fig. 3.12).
The lowest course of tiles at eaves edge is always
nailed, as are higher courses on a steep pitch.

Moreover, modern tiles today appear either to have
no need for a locking ring or to have only a shallow
ﬂ ange with a rectangular proﬁ le (Fig. 3.19).
    These observations suggest that the locking
ring was present in the early Ming, but may have
become less essential or even redundant at some
time before the mid Qing. Examination of a larger
sample of dateable examples may determine wheth-
er the changing design of locking rings and ﬂanges
might yield chronological markers.
  On roof edges, banwa and tongwa are modiﬁ ed
into eaves tiles, known collectively as wadang 䒎⻻,
whose integrally-moulded end-faces convert them
into drip tiles. The banwa is capped by a curved tri-
angular piece and becomes a dishui 㺜㯜, ‘a drip tile’
(Fig. 3.20), and the tongwa terminates with an inte-
grally moulded circular disc, the whole piece being
termed a goutou ⊦⣜, ‘a hook-ended tile’ (Fig. 3.21).
These are seen functioning together in Fig. 3.22.
   Archaeological evidence indicates that the gout-
ou ﬁrst evolved from combining a tongwa with a
separate semi-circular capping piece, which was re-
placed in the Qin and Han dynasties by a still-sepa-
rate circular piece that improved water-shedding.15
These were decorated with geometric designs or
silhouettes of animals.16 Although the separate cir-
cular end-piece continued to be used for some time,
an integral one-piece moulding with nail-hole had
already appeared by the Warring States period. An
impressively large example of such a goutou from
the Warring States period and excavated at the
Zhongshan necropolis at Pingshan, Hebei, is dis-
played at the Museum of the Society for Research in
Ancient Architecture in Beijing.17 This goutou is 80
centimetres long and signiﬁcantly larger than the
typical 36- to 37-centimetre length in widespread
use by the Ming dynasty, and it also shows an early

were discussed in Chapter 7. Ornament for walls is
usually applied as ‘tiles’, a term appropriate for
thin, ﬂat (and usually smaller) parts, which can be
distinguished from thicker (and larger) compo-
nents referred to in this book as ‘tile-bricks’. Tile-
bricks appear on dragon walls and, because of their
size, are made differently.
    Tiles appear generally in sizes up to about 35 cen-
timetres square with a thickness of 5 centimetres.
They are solid, ﬂat or moulded in relief, and glazed
on one face, or left unglazed. If small they have a ﬂat
back but larger pieces have a tongue or ﬂange on the
back which engages with a ﬁxing on the wall. Ob-
servation suggests that solid mouldings can be
made in moulded-relief up to 5 centimetres thick, in
sizes up to about 35 centimetres (though more often
smaller). Another type of solid moulding, but in
high relief, appears in high-relief decorative panels
on entrance screens in the Gugong (Fig. 8.20 and
Figs. 7.19 and 7.20). These are evidently modelled as
contoured ‘cut-outs’ applied to a ﬂat base.

   The dragon wall screens, which cover a period
from early Ming to mid-Qing tend to have no ‘rules’
about the number or positioning of ‘ﬂaming balls’
between them, except that the centre dragon, invari-
ably of an odd-numbered set, tends sometimes to be
presented frontally, cradling a ‘ﬂaming ball’, and this
motif also appears on late Ming ceramic ware.
  One ﬁnal observation on surviving dragon wall
screens (though too small a number to be consid-
ered a really representative sample)  is that the
‘rhythm’ of placement of the dragons tends to be al-
ternately head-up and head-down, with most head-
up dragons in ‘earth’ colours and those ‘head-down’
in semi-moribund posture. They are also ﬁnished in
other colours such as purple or a sickly pale buffcol-
our, and their tails are horizontally attenuated as if
suggesting the arrival of the creature at speed from a
distance. This design convention could have arisen
for purely aesthetic reasons but it is equally possible
that arrangement and colour conveyed some ‘mean-
ing’. If that is so, that meaning is not wholly evident
from those screens that survive.
